title: Charts: combo, formatting & sparklines
goal: Put two measures on one chart with a secondary axis, keep axes honest and charts uncluttered, and add sparklines.

steps.text:
A shop tracks **Revenue** (in the thousands) and **Margin %** (around 10 to 20) every month.

Put both on one chart with a single axis from 0 to 2400, and the Margin % line is a flat thread hugging the bottom. You can't see it rise or fall at all.

The fix is a **combo chart**: one measure gets its own axis. You'll build that idea, then learn to keep charts honest and clean, and finish with tiny charts that live inside a single cell.

steps.prompt: How bad is the mismatch? In ==D2==, work out how many times bigger January's Revenue is than its Margin %.
steps.explain: **100 times** bigger. On one axis that runs to 2400, a margin of 12 is half of one percent of the height: a flat line. Different scales need different axes.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the `/` sign and the cell names.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Divide January's Revenue (`B2`) by January's Margin % (`C2`).
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Use the Revenue and Margin % cells of January: `B2` and `C2`.

steps.prompt:
One of the two columns must move to a **secondary axis**, drawn on the right side of the chart.

Click the **letter** of the column whose numbers are being squashed, then press [[Enter]].
steps.wrongFeedback: Revenue's big numbers set the main axis. The column being squashed is the one with the **small** numbers: Margin %, column C.
clues: Which column's numbers are tiny next to the other?

steps.prompt:
Select the table and use **Insert → Combo chart**. Tick **Secondary Axis** next to one of the series.

Which setup tells the story best?
options: Both as columns on one axis
Revenue as columns, Margin % as a line on the secondary axis
Multiply every Margin % by 100 so it fits
steps.explain: **Columns for amounts, a line for a rate or percent**, with the line on the secondary axis. Different shapes also tell the reader which axis is which.
wrongFeedback: On one axis, the margin columns would be 1-pixel slivers. Nothing improves.
That hack changes your data to fit the chart, and the numbers on the axis stop meaning “%”. A secondary axis keeps the data true.
clues: Which setup keeps each measure's real numbers on an axis it can read?

steps.prompt:
Store A sold **80** and Store B sold **100**: B is 25% higher.

The chart's axis starts at **70** instead of 0. How many times taller will B's column look than A's?
steps.explain: Only the part **above** 70 is drawn: A shows 10 tall and B shows 30 tall, so B looks **3 times** taller. A 25% difference looks like 200%. Next, calculate it yourself.
wrongFeedback: That's the real ratio, which you only see if the axis starts at 0. Remember, bars only show the part above the axis start.
Don't compare 100 with 80 directly. Subtract what is cut off the bottom first.
clues: How tall is each bar above 70?

steps.prompt: In ==D2== calculate how many times taller B's bar looks. Each bar's height is its sales **minus** where the axis starts, which is in `C2`.
steps.explain: **3**. B is 30 above the axis start and A is 10, so B looks three times as tall, though it sold only 1.25 times as much.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the `/` sign.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Bar height = sales − axis start. Divide B's height by A's height.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: The axis start lives in `C2`. Use it.

clues: B's height is `B3-C2`; A's height is `B2-C2`.

steps.prompt:
Columns show **length**, so their axis must start at **0** (Format Axis → Minimum). Here the axis minimum is stored in `C2`.

Click ==C2==, type **0**, press [[Enter]] and watch `D2`.
steps.explain: At 0, the bars are 80 and 100, so B looks **1.25 times** as tall: the truth. Line charts may zoom in because they show position and trend, but a column's height must mean its size.

steps.prompt:
A one-series sales chart has a legend, thick gridlines, a 3-D effect and four colours. Everyone squints at it.

Which clean-up helps without losing information?
options: Add more colours and a 3-D effect so it stands out
Delete the legend, lighten the gridlines, switch off the 3-D effect
Delete the title and axis labels to make room
steps.explain: A legend for **one** series says nothing new, heavy gridlines fight the data, and 3-D distorts bar heights. Remove ink that carries no information, but keep the title and labels.
wrongFeedback: More decoration makes the data harder to read. 3-D also distorts the heights.
The title and labels carry meaning. Remove decoration, not information.
clues: What does each element tell the reader that they don't already know?

steps.prompt:
A **sparkline** is a tiny chart inside one cell, perfect for a trend beside each row.

Select Pune's four weeks, ==B2:E2==. Tap [[Alt]], [[N]], [[S]], [[L]] one after another (Insert → Sparklines → **Line**), choose `F2` as the location and press OK. Then drag `F2` down.

On a Mac: Insert → Sparklines → Line.
clues: Alt, N, S, then L for Line. (C is Column, W is Win/Loss.)

steps.prompt:
Chitra's weeks are **10, 20, 30, 40** and Dev's are **1000, 1100, 1200, 1300**. Both sparklines slope upward at a similar angle.

Does the same shape mean the same size?
options: Yes: same shape means same numbers
No: each sparkline scales itself. Set the same axis for all of them to compare size
No: sparklines can never be compared
steps.explain: Each sparkline zooms to its own minimum and maximum, so a tiny row and a huge row can look identical. On the **Sparkline** tab, **Axis → Same for All Sparklines** (for minimum and maximum) puts them on one scale. Use the default to compare shapes, and the common axis to compare sizes.
wrongFeedback: Look at the numbers: Dev's are 100 times bigger. The sparklines only look alike because each zooms to fit its own row.
They can be compared fairly once you fix a shared axis. That option exists.
clues: What scale does each sparkline use by default?

steps.prompt:
A column chart's axis starts at **400**, and the two bars are for last year's sales (450) and this year's (500).

How many times taller does this year's bar **look** than last year's? Put it in ==C2==.
steps.explain: **2**: the visible parts are 50 and 100, so this year looks twice as tall, although the real growth is only about 11%. If your chart does this, start the axis at 0.

wrongFeedback.parseError: Check the brackets and the `/` sign.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only the part above 400 is drawn. Compare 500 − 400 with 450 − 400.

clues: Bar heights: 50 and 100. Divide the second by the first.
